name: room
text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Run a quarterly audit of the top 20% of prompts by actual failure rate, not usage. This targets the highest-leverage fixes first, cutting waste where it hurts most. Trade-off: we ignore the other 80% of prompts, risking missed optimizations in less-frequent but still critical cases.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t false positives—it’s that a weekly score turns prompts into quarterly snapshots, missing the real waste: the 20% of prompts that fail *just* often enough to stay under the radar but *just* rarely enough to avoid detection. A better alternative is a rolling failure-rate window with a decay factor, so recent failures carry more weight than stale ones. Settle it by comparing the two methods on a 30-day slice of failure data—if the quarterly audit misses 15% more critical fixes than the rolling window, the quarterly approach fails.
